deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is §§7–8 of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (written 1854, published posthumously by Dedekind in 1867). This page is a fair copy of the published text.

(1) Setup, continued from the previous page. Put A_0 = b_0/2 and A_n = a_n sin nx + b_n cos nx. The series Ω = Σ_{n≥0} A_n is taken as given. Its value f(x) is defined only at those x where Ω converges.

(2) Case split. A necessary condition for convergence is A_n(x) → 0.
- If a_n, b_n → 0, then A_n(x) → 0 for every x, since |A_n(x)| ≤ sqrt(a_n² + b_n²).
- Otherwise A_n(x) → 0 can hold only for 'special' x.
The two cases are to be treated separately.

(3) §8, first case: A_n(x) → 0 for all x. Integrate Ω twice term by term:
- ∫∫ A_0 = A_0 x²/2.
- ∫∫ (a_n sin nx + b_n cos nx) = −A_n/n².
This gives F(x) = C + C'x + A_0 x²/2 − Σ_{n≥1} A_n/n².
Riemann claims three things:
- this series converges for every x;
- F is continuous;
- hence F is integrable everywhere.

(4) Proof of convergence. Let N be the partial sum up to −A_n/n² and R = −Σ_{m>n} A_m/m² the remainder. Let ε be the largest |A_m| for m > n. Then
|R| ≤ ε Σ_{m>n} 1/m² < ε/n.
The last step is implicit; I fill it: 1/m² < 1/(m(m−1)) = 1/(m−1) − 1/m, and the sum telescopes to 1/n. So the tail can be made arbitrarily small by taking n large, and the series converges (Cauchy criterion).

(5) Continuity. The argument begins at the foot of the page and ends on the next page. For a uniform choice of ε (independent of x), first take n so large that R is small for all x. Then take the change in x small enough that the finite sum N changes little. This is the standard uniform-convergence-implies-continuity argument.

Purpose: F is the function whose second symmetric difference quotient yields Riemann's Theorem 1 (on the next page). That theorem is the basis of Riemann's localization and uniqueness theory for trigonometric series.
errors: No real errors. ε is defined as 'the largest value of A_m for m>n' without saying explicitly that it must be taken as a bound uniform in x, e.g. sup_{m>n} sqrt(a_m²+b_m²). Pointwise, the bound only gives convergence at each x. The continuity argument on the next page ('was auch x sei') needs the uniform bound, which is available because a_n, b_n → 0 in this case.

The claim that otherwise A_n(x)→0 'can only happen for special values of x' is left as a heuristic here. The precise statement (if A_n(x)→0 on an interval, or on a set of positive measure, then a_n, b_n→0) is the Cantor–Lebesgue theorem: Cantor 1870 for intervals, Lebesgue later for positive measure.
The tail estimate Σ_{m>n} 1/m² < 1/n is stated without proof; it is correct, via telescoping.

results.what: Riemann function F(x) = C + C'x + A_0 x²/2 − Σ A_n/n², obtained by formal double termwise integration of a trigonometric series
results.modern_name: Riemann's (second) formal integral / Riemann function in uniqueness theory of trigonometric series

results.what: Convergence and continuity of F via the tail bound |R| ≤ ε Σ 1/m² < ε/n
results.modern_name: Weierstrass M-test / uniform convergence implies continuity

results.what: Case distinction according to whether a_n, b_n → 0; remark that otherwise A_n(x)→0 only for special x

deep.surprise_reason: This is a manuscript of the published Habilitationsschrift (§§7–8), whose content is universally known and credited to Riemann.

checkable.asserts: Twice differentiating −A_n/n² gives back A_n (should be 0)
The constant term integrates twice to A_0 x²/2 + C + C'x (should be 0)
The telescoping majorant sum equals 1/n, so Σ_{m>n} 1/m² < 1/n
The tail of Σ 1/m² is less than 1/n for sample n
